decks.title: Activation Energy, Collision Theory and Arrhenius Equation — Part 1: Energy barriers and collisions
goals: Explain energy barrier, threshold energy, activation energy and the activated complex
Draw and label energy profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, with and without a catalyst
Explain why only a fraction of collisions lead to reaction (energy and orientation)

slides.heading: Why reactions need a push
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the energy barrier that molecules must cross, and why most collisions fail.

rows: A matchstick needs striking before it burns
Energy is needed to start the reaction (activation energy)
More molecules have enough energy at higher temperature

visual.alt: Table of everyday observations explained by activation energy

slides.narration: Namaste! A matchstick and the oxygen in air could react, yet the match lies quietly in its box until you strike it. Why? Because reactions must overcome an energy barrier before they can proceed. In this part we meet that barrier, the activation energy, see it on energy profile diagrams, and use collision theory to understand why only a small fraction of molecular collisions actually lead to reaction.

slides.heading: Threshold energy and activation energy
slides.body_md: **Threshold energy:** the minimum total energy that colliding molecules must have for the collision to produce a reaction. **Activation energy (Ea):** the extra energy that must be supplied to reactant molecules, beyond their average energy, to reach the threshold energy: Ea = threshold energy − average energy of reactants. **Activated complex:** the unstable, high-energy arrangement at the top of the barrier, in which old bonds are partly broken and new ones partly formed.

rows: The hump between reactants and products on an energy profile
Energy level at the top of the barrier
Height of the barrier above the reactants
Short-lived species at the top; bonds partly broken and formed

visual.alt: Table of terms used for the energy barrier

slides.narration: Reactant molecules must reach a certain minimum energy, the threshold energy, before they can rearrange into products. The extra energy they need above their average energy is the activation energy. At the top of the barrier they form an activated complex, an unstable arrangement in which old bonds are stretched and new bonds are half formed; it can fall forward to products or back to reactants.

slides.heading: Energy profile of an exothermic reaction
slides.body_md: Products lie **below** the reactants (ΔH < 0). The reactants must still climb over the barrier. A **catalyst** (dashed path) provides a route with a **lower** activation energy; it does not change the energies of reactants and products, so ΔH is unchanged.

slides.narration: In an exothermic reaction the products have less energy than the reactants, so heat is released overall. Even so, the molecules must first climb a hill to form the activated complex. The height of that climb, measured from the reactants, is the activation energy. With a catalyst, shown dashed, the hill is lower, but the starting and finishing levels, and so the enthalpy change, stay the same.

slides.narration: In an endothermic reaction the products lie higher than the reactants, so heat is absorbed overall. The barrier is measured from the reactants for the forward reaction and from the products for the reverse reaction. The difference between the two activation energies equals the enthalpy change, so for an endothermic reaction the forward activation energy is always larger than the enthalpy change.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading an energy profile
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For a reaction, the reactants are at 40 kJ mol⁻¹, the activated complex at 160 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 100 kJ mol⁻¹ (all on the same scale). Find (a) Ea(forward), (b) Ea(reverse) and (c) ΔH; state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

**(a)** $E_\text{a(f)} = 160 - 40 = 120\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**(b)** $E_\text{a(r)} = 160 - 100 = 60\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**(c)** $\Delta H = 100 - 40 = +60\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (= 120 − 60): endothermic.

visual.alt: Table of activation energies and enthalpy change from the energy profile

slides.narration: Measure everything from the right level. The forward activation energy is the height of the activated complex above the reactants, one hundred and twenty. The reverse activation energy is its height above the products, sixty. The enthalpy change is products minus reactants, plus sixty, which also equals the difference between the two activation energies. A positive value means the reaction is endothermic.

slides.heading: Quick check: energy profiles
slides.body_md: Use an energy profile to find an activation energy or the enthalpy change.
slides.narration: Quick check. Forward activation energy is measured from the reactants; the enthalpy change is products minus reactants.

slides.heading: Effect of a catalyst
slides.body_md: A **catalyst** provides an alternative pathway (mechanism) with a **lower activation energy**. It lowers Ea for the forward and reverse reactions **equally**, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position is unchanged. It does not alter ΔH, ΔG or K and is regenerated at the end.

rows: Lower Ea of forward and reverse reactions
Increase the fraction of effective collisions
Change the equilibrium constant or yield
Take part in the mechanism and come out unchanged

visual.alt: Table of what a catalyst does and does not do

slides.narration: A catalyst is like a tunnel through the hill: the start and the finish are the same, but the climb is lower. More molecules now have enough energy to get over, so the reaction speeds up. Because the forward and reverse barriers are lowered by the same amount, equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium constant, the enthalpy change and the Gibbs energy change are not altered.

slides.heading: Quick check: catalysts and energy
slides.body_md: Decide which quantity a catalyst changes.
slides.narration: Quick check. A catalyst lowers the barrier but leaves the starting and finishing energy levels unchanged.

slides.heading: Collision theory
slides.body_md: Reacting molecules are pictured as hard spheres that must **collide**. A collision is **effective** only if (i) the colliding molecules have energy at least equal to the **threshold energy**, and (ii) they collide with **proper orientation**. Rate ∝ collision frequency × fraction of collisions with enough energy × orientation (steric) factor.

rows: Enough energy to stretch and break bonds
Reacting atoms must come into contact
Only a tiny fraction meet both conditions

visual.alt: Table of the conditions for an effective collision

slides.narration: Collision theory says molecules must collide to react, but colliding is not enough. In a gas, each molecule collides billions of times a second, yet many reactions are slow. A collision works only if the molecules carry at least the threshold energy and meet in the right orientation. The rate depends on how often molecules collide, the fraction with enough energy, and the probability of the right orientation.

slides.heading: Orientation matters
slides.body_md: When OH⁻ reacts with CH₃Br, it must strike the carbon atom from the side **opposite** the bromine. A collision at the bromine end is ineffective, however energetic.

slides.narration: Here is an example of orientation. A hydroxide ion can replace the bromine in bromomethane only if it approaches the carbon atom from the side opposite the bromine. If it strikes the bromine end, the two simply bounce apart. This need for the right orientation is why the steric factor in collision theory is often much less than one.

slides.heading: Worked example: effective collisions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In a gas reaction at 300 K, $Z = 1.0 \times 10^{31}$ collisions per litre per second, the fraction with enough energy is $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT} = 2.0 \times 10^{-9}$ and the steric factor is $0.05$. How many effective collisions occur per litre per second?

**Step 1.** Energetic collisions $= 1.0 \times 10^{31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-9} = 2.0 \times 10^{22}$.

**Step 2.** Effective collisions $= 2.0 \times 10^{22} \times 0.05 = 1.0 \times 10^{21}$ per litre per second.

visual.alt: Flow from total collisions to effective collisions

slides.narration: Start with all the collisions, ten to the thirty one per litre per second. Only two in a thousand million carry enough energy, which leaves two times ten to the twenty two. Of those, only one in twenty is correctly oriented, giving ten to the twenty one effective collisions. Even this is a huge number, but it is a tiny fraction of all collisions.

slides.heading: Effect of temperature on collisions
slides.body_md: Raising the temperature increases the collision frequency only slightly, but it greatly increases the **fraction of molecules with energy ≥ threshold** (the tail of the energy distribution). That is why a 10 K rise often roughly doubles the rate.

visual.alt: Distribution of molecular kinetic energies at two temperatures: at the higher temperature the curve is flatter and spread to higher energies, so a larger fraction of molecules lies beyond the activation energy line
visual.caption: Illustrative curves; the temperature gap is exaggerated so that the difference is visible.

slides.narration: At any temperature molecules have a spread of energies. Only those beyond the activation energy line can react. When the temperature rises by ten kelvin, the curve flattens and shifts to higher energies, and the small tail beyond the line grows a lot, often doubling. The molecules also move a little faster, but the growing tail is the main reason reactions speed up so much on warming.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Ea = threshold energy − average energy of reactants; activated complex at the top of the barrier.
Exothermic: products below reactants; endothermic: products above; ΔH = Ea(f) − Ea(r).
A catalyst lowers Ea (forward and reverse equally); ΔH, ΔG and K unchanged.
Effective collisions need energy ≥ threshold and proper orientation.
Temperature mainly raises the fraction of energetic molecules.

visual.alt: Summary table of quantities on an energy profile

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Reactants must reach the threshold energy to form the activated complex; the extra energy needed is the activation energy. Energy profiles show this for exothermic and endothermic reactions, and a catalyst lowers the barrier without changing the enthalpy change. Collision theory explains that only energetic, well-oriented collisions succeed, and temperature mainly increases the energetic fraction.

decks.title: Activation Energy, Collision Theory and Arrhenius Equation — Part 2: The Arrhenius equation
goals: State the Arrhenius equation and explain the meaning of A and Ea
Use the log form and the graph of log k against 1/T to find Ea and A
Calculate activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures
Calculate the effect of a catalyst or a temperature change on the rate constant

slides.heading: The Arrhenius equation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — putting numbers to the effect of temperature on rate.

visual.alt: Flow of topics in Part 2

slides.narration: Why does food keep for days in a refrigerator but spoil in hours in summer? In eighteen eighty nine Svante Arrhenius gave an equation connecting the rate constant with temperature and the activation energy. In this part we use it in its exponential and logarithmic forms, read activation energies from graphs, and solve the numericals that ISC papers often set.

slides.heading: The Arrhenius equation
slides.body_md: $k = A\,e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$. **A** is the **frequency (pre-exponential) factor**, related to the frequency of collisions with proper orientation; it has the same unit as $k$. $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ is the **fraction of molecules** with energy at least $E_\text{a}$ (the Boltzmann factor). A larger $E_\text{a}$ gives a smaller $k$ and a reaction more sensitive to temperature.

rows: Fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea

visual.alt: Table of terms in the Arrhenius equation

slides.narration: In the Arrhenius equation, the rate constant equals A times e to the power minus activation energy over R T. A is the frequency factor, which counts collisions with the right orientation. The exponential term is the fraction of molecules with at least the activation energy. Because the activation energy sits in the exponent, small changes in temperature or activation energy change the rate constant enormously.

slides.heading: Log form and the Arrhenius plot
slides.body_md: Taking logarithms: $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{RT}$, or $\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303RT}$. A plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ is a straight line with **slope $= -E_\text{a}/2.303R$** and **intercept $= \log A$**.

visual.alt: Arrhenius plot: log of the rate constant against one thousand divided by temperature is a straight line sloping downwards; the slope gives the activation energy and the intercept gives the frequency factor
visual.caption: Illustrative line: slope −4000 K (per unit of 1/T), so Ea = 2.303 × 8.314 × 4000 ≈ 76.6 kJ mol⁻¹; intercept log A = 11.

slides.narration: Taking logs turns the exponential equation into a straight line. If you plot log k against one over T, the points fall on a line sloping downwards. The slope is minus the activation energy divided by two point three zero three R, so measuring the slope gives the activation energy. Extending the line to where one over T is zero gives log A, the frequency factor.

slides.heading: Worked example: Ea and A from an Arrhenius plot
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ for a reaction is a straight line with slope $-5000\ \text{K}$ and intercept $12.0$ ($k$ in s⁻¹). Find $E_\text{a}$ and $A$.

**Step 1.** $-\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R} = -5000$, so $E_\text{a} = 5000 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \approx 95\,740\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, i.e. about $95.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\log A = 12.0$, so $A = 1.0 \times 10^{12}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of Arrhenius plot values and results

slides.narration: The slope equals minus the activation energy over two point three zero three R. Multiplying five thousand by two point three zero three and by eight point three one four gives about ninety six thousand joules, so the activation energy is about ninety six kilojoules per mole. The intercept is log A, twelve, so A is ten to the twelve per second, the same unit as the first-order rate constant.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Arrhenius plot
slides.body_md: Interpret the slope or intercept of a graph of log k against 1/T.
slides.narration: Quick check. The slope gives the activation energy and the intercept gives the frequency factor.

slides.heading: Rate constants at two temperatures
slides.body_md: Writing the log form at $T_1$ and $T_2$ and subtracting removes $A$:

visual.alt: Table of uses of the two-temperature Arrhenius equation

slides.narration: If we know the rate constant at two temperatures, we can find the activation energy without knowing A: write the log form for each temperature and subtract, and A cancels. The same equation, rearranged, gives the rate constant at a new temperature or the temperature needed for a desired rate constant. Remember to use kelvin and joules.

slides.heading: Worked example: activation energy from two rate constants
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The rate constant of a first-order reaction is $2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$ and $8.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $320\ \text{K}$. Calculate $E_\text{a}$ ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$).

**Step 1.** $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \log 4 = 0.602$.

**Step 2.** $\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2} = \dfrac{20}{300 \times 320} = 2.083 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

**Step 3.** $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.602}{2.083 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 55\,340\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, i.e. about $55.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps for finding Ea from two rate constants

slides.narration: The rate constant becomes four times larger, and log four is about nought point six. The temperature term is twenty divided by three hundred times three hundred and twenty. Rearranging for the activation energy and putting in two point three zero three times the gas constant gives about fifty five kilojoules per mole. Notice that a twenty kelvin rise quadrupled the rate: roughly doubling for every ten kelvin.

slides.heading: Worked example: a new rate constant
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A reaction has $E_\text{a} = 60.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $k = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $310\ \text{K}$. Calculate $k$ at $330\ \text{K}$.

**Step 1.** $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{60000}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{310 \times 330} \approx 3133.6 \times 1.955 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.613$.

**Step 2.** $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 10^{0.613} \approx 4.10$; $k_2 \approx 4.10 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \approx 6.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of rate constants at two temperatures

slides.narration: Put the activation energy in joules, sixty thousand. The first factor, sixty thousand over two point three zero three R, is about three thousand one hundred and thirty four. The temperature factor is twenty over three hundred and ten times three hundred and thirty. Their product, about nought point six one, is the log of the ratio, so the rate constant rises about four times, to six point two thousandths per second.

slides.heading: Quick check: temperature and k
slides.body_md: Predict how k changes with temperature or with activation energy.
slides.narration: Quick check. A reaction with a higher activation energy is more sensitive to temperature.

slides.heading: Temperature coefficient
slides.body_md: The **temperature coefficient** is the ratio of rate constants at two temperatures 10 K apart, usually $k_{308}/k_{298}$. For many reactions it is about **2 to 3**. It is larger for reactions with a larger activation energy.

visual.alt: Table of approximate temperature coefficients for different activation energies

slides.narration: Chemists often quote the temperature coefficient, the factor by which the rate constant increases for a ten kelvin rise, usually from twenty five to thirty five degrees Celsius. For many reactions it is two or three. A reaction with an activation energy of about fifty three kilojoules per mole doubles its rate for a ten kelvin rise; one with a larger activation energy speeds up even more.

slides.heading: Worked example: effect of a catalyst
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At 300 K, an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction from $80$ to $55\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. If $A$ is unchanged, by what factor does the rate increase?

**Step 1.** $\log\dfrac{k_\text{cat}}{k} = \dfrac{E_\text{a} - E'_\text{a}}{2.303RT} = \dfrac{25000}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300} = \dfrac{25000}{5744} = 4.35$.

**Step 2.** $\dfrac{k_\text{cat}}{k} = 10^{4.35} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{4}$.

visual.alt: Table comparing rate constants with and without the enzyme

slides.narration: Because A is the same, dividing the two Arrhenius equations leaves only the exponential terms. Lowering the activation energy by twenty five kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin raises log k by about four point three five, so the reaction goes about twenty two thousand times faster. That is how enzymes let reactions in our bodies proceed quickly at body temperature.

slides.narration: Quick check. Use kelvin for temperature and joules for activation energy with R equal to eight point three one four.

A plot of log k against one over T gives the activation energy from its slope and A from its intercept. The two-temperature form finds the activation energy or a new rate constant, and shows why catalysts and temperature have such large effects.

Put the higher temperature second so the log is positive. And for a plot of common logs, the slope is minus the activation energy over two point three zero three R.

sections.heading: 1. Energy barrier, threshold energy and activation energy
sections.body_md:
Reactants must cross an **energy barrier** to become products. **Threshold energy:** the minimum energy colliding molecules must have to react. **Activation energy** $E_\text{a}$ = threshold energy − average energy of the reactants. **Activated complex:** the unstable, high-energy arrangement at the top of the barrier (bonds partly broken and partly formed); it may give products or revert to reactants.

Lower $E_\text{a}$ → faster reaction at a given temperature.

key_terms.definition_md: The minimum energy that colliding molecules must possess for the collision to result in reaction.
The extra energy, above the average energy of reactants, needed to reach the threshold energy.
The unstable species at the top of the energy barrier.

sections.heading: 2. Energy profiles; effect of a catalyst
sections.body_md:
**Exothermic:** products below reactants, $\Delta H < 0$. **Endothermic:** products above reactants, $\Delta H > 0$. In all cases $\Delta H = E_\text{a(forward)} - E_\text{a(reverse)}$, so for an endothermic reaction $E_\text{a(f)} > \Delta H$.

**Catalyst:** provides an alternative path of lower $E_\text{a}$ for both forward and reverse reactions; does not change ΔH, ΔG, K or the position of equilibrium; is regenerated; equilibrium is reached sooner. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that increases the rate by providing a path of lower activation energy and is regenerated at the end.

sections.heading: 3. Collision theory
sections.body_md:
Reactant molecules (treated as hard spheres) must collide. A collision is **effective** only if (i) the energy of the colliding molecules is at least the threshold energy and (ii) the molecules have the **proper orientation**. Rate $= P\,Z_\text{AB}\,e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$: $Z_\text{AB}$ = collision frequency, $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ = fraction of collisions with enough energy, $P$ = probability (steric) factor.

Raising temperature increases the collision frequency slightly but the **fraction of energetic molecules** greatly (tail of the energy distribution), so the rate rises sharply. (The mathematical treatment of collision theory is not required.)

key_terms.definition_md: A collision with energy at least equal to the threshold energy and proper orientation, which leads to reaction.
The probability that a collision has the proper orientation.

sections.heading: 4. The Arrhenius equation
sections.body_md:
$k = A\,e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$: $A$ = frequency (pre-exponential) factor (same unit as $k$); $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ = fraction of molecules with energy ≥ $E_\text{a}$.

Log form: $\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303RT}$. Plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$: straight line, **slope $= -E_\text{a}/2.303R$**, **intercept $= \log A$**.

Two temperatures: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$.

**Temperature coefficient** $= k_{T+10}/k_T$, usually 2–3; larger for larger $E_\text{a}$. A catalyst lowering $E_\text{a}$ by $\Delta E_\text{a}$ (same $A$) multiplies $k$ by $10^{\Delta E_\text{a}/2.303RT}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The pre-exponential constant A in the Arrhenius equation, related to the frequency of correctly oriented collisions.
Ratio of rate constants at two temperatures differing by 10 K.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Measuring activation energy from zero energy instead of from the reactant level.
- Saying a catalyst changes ΔH, ΔG or the equilibrium constant.
- Using °C, or Ea in kJ with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, in Arrhenius calculations.
- Using slope = −Ea/R for a plot of log₁₀ k (it is −Ea/2.303R).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Energy profiles (2 marks): axes, reactant and product levels, activated complex, Ea and ΔH labelled; catalysed path lower.
- Collision theory (2 marks): both conditions for an effective collision.
- Arrhenius numericals (3 marks): correct equation, substitution with units in J and K, answer in kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: On the energy profile of a reaction, the reactants are at 30 kJ mol⁻¹, the activated complex at 130 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at −20 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy of the forward reaction is:
questions.solution_md: Ea(f) = 130 − 30 = 100 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (a); 150 is Ea of the reverse reaction (b).

questions.stem_md: In the Haber process, finely divided iron speeds up N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Which quantity does the iron catalyst change?

options.text_md: The enthalpy change of the reaction
The activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions
The Gibbs energy change of the reaction

questions.solution_md: A catalyst provides a lower-energy path; ΔH, ΔG and K are unchanged — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For the reaction between hydrogen and iodine molecules, the minimum energy that colliding molecules must possess for the collision to produce HI is called the:
questions.solution_md: The minimum energy for reaction is the threshold energy; activation energy is the extra energy above the average (a) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the reaction OH⁻ + CH₃Br → CH₃OH + Br⁻, the species HO···CH₃···Br at the top of the energy barrier is best described as:

options.text_md: an activated complex in which the C–O bond is forming while the C–Br bond is breaking
a stable intermediate that can be isolated

questions.solution_md: The activated complex is a short-lived arrangement at the energy maximum with bonds partly made and broken — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For the endothermic decomposition of calcium carbonate, which relation between the activation energies is correct?
questions.solution_md: ΔH = Ea(f) − Ea(r) > 0, so Ea(f) > Ea(r) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A matchstick does not catch fire in its box but bursts into flame when struck. The best explanation is:

options.text_md: combustion of the match head is endothermic until it is struck
striking supplies the activation energy needed to start the combustion

questions.solution_md: The reaction is already exothermic and spontaneous, but the molecules must first cross the energy barrier — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The enzyme catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide in a cut millions of times faster than it decomposes on its own. This is because catalase:

options.text_md: provides a reaction path with a much lower activation energy
raises the temperature of the wound

questions.solution_md: Enzymes are catalysts: they lower Ea without changing ΔH or K — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a reaction, Ea(forward) = 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy of the reverse reaction is:
questions.solution_md: Ea(r) = Ea(f) − ΔH = 80 − 30 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Platinum gauze increases the rate of the forward reaction in 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ by a factor of 1000 at a given temperature. The rate of the reverse reaction is increased by a factor of:
questions.solution_md: A catalyst lowers both activation energies equally, so both rate constants rise by the same factor and K is unchanged — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Adding vanadium(V) oxide to the contact process does not change the equilibrium yield of SO₃.

**Reason (R):** A catalyst lowers the activation energies of the forward and reverse reactions equally.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: equal speeding up of both directions leaves K unchanged — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For an endothermic reaction such as the decomposition of N₂O₄ into NO₂, the forward activation energy can be smaller than ΔH.

**Reason (R):** ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: since Ea(reverse) is positive, Ea(forward) = ΔH + Ea(reverse) > ΔH. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The activated complex formed when H₂ and I₂ react can be isolated and stored like a normal compound.
questions.solution_md: False. The activated complex exists only at the energy maximum for an instant; it cannot be isolated.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Manganese dioxide makes the decomposition of potassium chlorate faster but does not change ΔG for the reaction.
questions.solution_md: True. A catalyst changes the path, not the energies of reactants and products.

questions.stem_md: The extra energy that reactant molecules must absorb, above their average energy, to reach the threshold energy is called the ___ energy.
questions.solution_md: The **activation** energy.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature of the energy profile for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g) with its description.

options.text_md: The highest point of the curve
Height of the peak above the reactants
Height of the peak above the products
Difference between reactant and product levels

match_right.text_md: Activation energy of the forward reaction
Activation energy of the reverse reaction

questions.solution_md: Peak → activated complex; reactants→peak → Ea(f); products→peak → Ea(r); reactants→products → ΔH.

questions.stem_md: The decomposition of an organic peroxide has Ea(forward) = 150 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction, in kJ mol⁻¹?
Sketch and label the energy profile for the exothermic combustion of methane, showing the paths with and without a catalyst.

answer.model_answer_md: Energy (y-axis) against reaction coordinate (x-axis). The reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂) start at a higher level and the products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) end at a lower level, so ΔH is negative. The uncatalysed path rises to a tall peak (the activated complex); Ea is measured from the reactant level to this peak. The catalysed path, drawn dashed, has a lower peak (smaller Ea′) but the same starting and finishing levels.

questions.solution_md: Labelled profile with two humps.

marking_scheme.step: Peak, Ea and lower catalysed path

questions.stem_md: Explain why, for the endothermic reaction N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), the activation energy of the forward reaction must be greater than ΔH.

answer.model_answer_md: On the energy profile, the products lie above the reactants by ΔH, and the activated complex lies above the products by Ea(reverse), which is positive. Ea(forward) is the height from the reactants to the peak, so Ea(f) = ΔH + Ea(r), which is greater than ΔH.

questions.solution_md: Ea(f) = ΔH + Ea(r).

questions.stem_md: Explain why adding a catalyst to the reversible esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol makes equilibrium be reached sooner but does not change the equilibrium constant.

answer.model_answer_md: The catalyst (H⁺) provides an alternative path that lowers the activation energy of both the forward and the reverse reaction by the same amount, so both rates increase by the same factor and equilibrium is reached sooner. Because K = k(forward)/k(reverse), and both rate constants increase equally, K is unchanged; ΔG and ΔH are also unaffected.

questions.solution_md: Equal effect on both directions.

marking_scheme.step: Lowers Ea of both directions equally

questions.stem_md: For the reaction A + B → C + D, the energies (kJ mol⁻¹) are: reactants 50, activated complex 170, products 90. A catalyst lowers the peak to 120. Calculate (a) Ea(forward) and Ea(reverse) without the catalyst, (b) the same with the catalyst and (c) ΔH in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Ea(f) = 170 − 50 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹; Ea(r) = 170 − 90 = 80 kJ mol⁻¹. (b) Ea(f) = 120 − 50 = 70 kJ mol⁻¹; Ea(r) = 120 − 90 = 30 kJ mol⁻¹ (both lowered by 50). (c) ΔH = 90 − 50 = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ in both cases (endothermic); the catalyst does not change ΔH.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define threshold energy, activation energy and activated complex. [1½]

(b) Draw labelled energy profiles for (i) an exothermic reaction and (ii) an endothermic reaction, each with and without a catalyst. [2]

(c) For a reaction, Ea(forward) = 96 kJ mol⁻¹ and Ea(reverse) = 128 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔH and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Threshold energy: the minimum energy colliding molecules must have to react. Activation energy: the extra energy, above the average energy of the reactants, needed to reach the threshold. Activated complex: the unstable arrangement at the top of the barrier with bonds partly broken and formed. (b) (i) Products below reactants, ΔH < 0, peak above both; catalysed (dashed) peak lower, ends unchanged. (ii) Products above reactants, ΔH > 0; Ea(f) greater than ΔH; catalysed peak lower, ends unchanged. Ea is measured from the reactant level in each. (c) ΔH = Ea(f) − Ea(r) = 96 − 128 = −32 kJ mol⁻¹: exothermic.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; profiles; −32 kJ/mol, exothermic.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain, with an energy profile, how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. State three things a catalyst does not change. [3]

(b) The enzyme invertase lowers the activation energy for the hydrolysis of sucrose from 107 kJ mol⁻¹ to 36 kJ mol⁻¹. Assuming A is unchanged, calculate the factor by which the rate increases at 310 K. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A catalyst provides an alternative path with a lower peak on the energy profile, so a larger fraction of molecules has enough energy to react; the starting and finishing levels are unchanged. It does not change ΔH, ΔG or the equilibrium constant (nor the position of equilibrium).

(b) $\log\dfrac{k_\text{cat}}{k} = \dfrac{\Delta E_\text{a}}{2.303RT} = \dfrac{71000}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 310} \approx 11.96$, so the rate increases by about $10^{12}$ ($9.1 \times 10^{11}$) times.

questions.solution_md: Lower peak; ΔH, ΔG, K unchanged; about 10¹² times.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Lower activation energy path with profile

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen and iodine molecules in a flask at 600 K collide billions of times a second, yet HI forms only slowly. The main reason is that most collisions:

options.text_md: occur between molecules of the same gas only
take place at the walls of the flask
lack the threshold energy or the proper orientation

questions.solution_md: Only collisions with enough energy and the right orientation are effective — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A hydroxide ion collides with a bromomethane molecule with more than the threshold energy, but no reaction occurs. The most likely reason is that:

options.text_md: the OH⁻ ion struck the bromine end instead of the carbon atom opposite the bromine
the collision had too much energy

questions.solution_md: Even energetic collisions fail without proper orientation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: When the temperature of a mixture of H₂ and Cl₂ in the dark is raised by 10 K, the rate roughly doubles. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: the fraction of molecules with energy above the threshold increases greatly
the number of collisions per second doubles

questions.solution_md: Collision frequency rises only a few per cent; the energetic fraction (tail of the distribution) roughly doubles — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid that reacts with marble chips increases the rate mainly because it increases:

options.text_md: the number of collisions per second
the fraction of collisions with enough energy
the proportion of correctly oriented collisions

questions.solution_md: More acid particles per unit volume means more collisions; the energy distribution is unchanged at the same temperature — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a reaction between two large, complex organic molecules, the probability (steric) factor P in collision theory is usually:

options.text_md: much less than 1, because only a small part of each molecule can react

questions.solution_md: Most orientations bring unreactive parts together, so only a small fraction of collisions are correctly oriented — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Not every collision between H₂ and I₂ molecules produces hydrogen iodide.

**Reason (R):** Many collisions do not have the threshold energy or the proper orientation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For many reactions, a 10 K rise in temperature roughly doubles the rate.

**Reason (R):** A 10 K rise in temperature doubles the collision frequency.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — collision frequency rises only by about 2%; it is the fraction of energetic molecules that roughly doubles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the reaction of OH⁻ with CH₃Br, a collision with enough energy can still fail if the ion strikes the bromine end of the molecule.
questions.solution_md: True. Proper orientation is the second condition for an effective collision.

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions for a collision between nitrogen monoxide and ozone molecules to be effective in forming NO₂ and O₂.

answer.model_answer_md: The colliding molecules must have energy equal to or greater than the threshold energy, so that bonds can be broken; and they must collide with the proper orientation, so that the O atom of ozone meets the N atom of nitrogen monoxide.

questions.solution_md: Energy and orientation.

questions.stem_md: Using the distribution of molecular energies, explain why a 10 K rise in temperature roughly doubles the rate of the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: At the higher temperature the energy distribution curve flattens and shifts to higher energies. The area under the curve beyond the activation energy — the fraction of molecules with enough energy to react — roughly doubles, although the collision frequency rises only slightly. So the number of effective collisions, and the rate, roughly doubles.

questions.solution_md: Energetic fraction doubles.

marking_scheme.step: Curve shifts; fraction beyond Ea increases
Roughly doubles; collision frequency hardly changes

questions.stem_md: Use collision theory to explain how each change affects the rate of the reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid: (a) using more concentrated acid, (b) warming the acid, (c) adding a few drops of copper sulfate solution as a catalyst.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) More acid particles per unit volume increases the number of collisions per second, so the number of effective collisions and the rate increase. (b) Warming increases the fraction of particles with energy above the threshold (and slightly the collision frequency), so the rate increases sharply. (c) A catalyst provides a path of lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react, increasing the rate.

questions.solution_md: Collision frequency; energetic fraction; lower Ea.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the main postulates of collision theory, including the two conditions for an effective collision. [2]

(b) Sketch the distribution of kinetic energies of gas molecules at two temperatures, mark the activation energy, and use it to explain the effect of temperature on rate. [2]

(c) Give one limitation of collision theory. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Reactant molecules, treated as hard spheres, must collide to react; the rate depends on the collision frequency. A collision is effective only if the molecules have energy at least equal to the threshold energy and collide with proper orientation; rate = P Z e^(−Ea/RT). (b) The curve at the higher temperature is flatter and spread to higher energies; the shaded area beyond the Ea line (fraction of molecules able to react) is much larger, so the number of effective collisions and the rate increase greatly, even though the collision frequency increases only slightly. (c) It treats molecules as hard spheres and ignores their structure; the steric factor P has to be introduced empirically.

questions.solution_md: Postulates; distribution; limitation.

questions.stem_md: For the decomposition of acetaldehyde, a graph of log k against 1/T is a straight line. Its slope is equal to:
questions.solution_md: log k = log A − (Ea/2.303R)(1/T) — option (b); −Ea/R is the slope for ln k (a); log A is the intercept (c).

questions.stem_md: Reaction P has Ea = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ and reaction Q has Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹. When both are warmed from 300 K to 310 K:

options.text_md: the rate constant of P increases by a larger factor than that of Q
both increase by the same factor
the rate constant of Q decreases
the rate constant of Q increases by a larger factor than that of P

questions.solution_md: log(k₂/k₁) is proportional to Ea, so the reaction with the larger Ea is more temperature-sensitive — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which equation correctly relates the rate constants k₁ and k₂ of the decomposition of N₂O₅ at temperatures T₁ and T₂ (T₂ > T₁)?
questions.solution_md: Subtracting the log forms at T₁ and T₂ gives option (b).

questions.stem_md: For the first-order decomposition of cyclopropane to propene, the frequency factor A has the unit:
questions.solution_md: A has the same unit as k; for a first-order reaction that is s⁻¹ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: According to the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), as the temperature becomes very high the rate constant approaches:
questions.solution_md: As T → ∞, Ea/RT → 0 and e^0 = 1, so k → A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The temperature coefficient of the hydrolysis of an ester, k(308 K)/k(298 K), is found to be 2. This means that:

options.text_md: the rate constant doubles for a 10 K rise in temperature
the rate halves for a 10 K rise

questions.solution_md: The temperature coefficient is the ratio of rate constants 10 K apart — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Some radical recombination reactions, such as 2CH₃• → C₂H₆, have an activation energy close to zero. For such a reaction, the rate constant:
questions.solution_md: With Ea ≈ 0, k ≈ A, which is almost independent of temperature — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student plots ln k (natural logarithm) instead of log k against 1/T for the decomposition of hydrogen iodide. The slope of her graph is:
questions.solution_md: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rate of a reaction with a large activation energy is very sensitive to temperature.

**Reason (R):** The frequency factor A is almost independent of temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A; the sensitivity arises because Ea appears in the exponent e^(−Ea/RT) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? For the decomposition of N₂O₅, which has a positive activation energy, the rate constant increases as the temperature rises.
questions.solution_md: True. With Ea > 0, e^(−Ea/RT) increases with T, so k increases.

questions.stem_md: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT), the constant A is called the ___ factor.
questions.solution_md: The **frequency** (pre-exponential) factor.

questions.stem_md: Match each term in the Arrhenius treatment of the decomposition of N₂O₅ with its meaning.

match_right.text_md: Fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea
Minimum extra energy needed for reaction
Frequency factor, related to correctly oriented collisions

questions.solution_md: A → frequency factor; Ea → activation energy; exponential → energetic fraction; slope → −Ea/2.303R.

questions.stem_md: The rate constant of the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester doubles when the temperature is raised from $300\ \text{K}$ to $310\ \text{K}$. Calculate the activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\log 2 = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R} \times \dfrac{10}{300 \times 310}$, so $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.301 \times 93000}{10} \approx 53\,600\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$; in kJ: $53600 \div 1000 = 53.6$.

questions.stem_md: A reaction has $E_\text{a} = 50.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$. Calculate $k$ at $350\ \text{K}$, in units of $10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution_md: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{50000}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{50}{300 \times 350} \approx 2611.4 \times 4.762 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.2435$; $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} \approx 17.5$; $k_2 \approx 17.5 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-5} = 3.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$; in units of $10^{-4}$: $3.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{4} = 3.5$.

questions.stem_md: A first-order reaction has $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $400\ \text{K}$ and $E_\text{a} = 40.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the frequency factor $A$ in s⁻¹.
For the decomposition of nitrous oxide on gold, a plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ has a slope of $-6000\ \text{K}$. Calculate $E_\text{a}$ in kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $E_\text{a} = 2.303R \times 6000 = 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 6000 \approx 114\,880\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$; in kJ: $E_\text{a} = 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 6000 \div 1000 \approx 114.9\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: At $310\ \text{K}$ an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction by $20.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Assuming $A$ is unchanged, by what factor does the rate constant increase?
questions.solution_md: $\log\dfrac{k_\text{cat}}{k} = \dfrac{20000}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 310} \approx \dfrac{20000}{5935.6} \approx 3.3695$; factor $= 10^{3.3695} \approx 2342$ (about $2.3 \times 10^{3}$).

questions.stem_md: A reaction with $E_\text{a} = 70.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ has a rate constant $k$ at $300\ \text{K}$. At what temperature, in K, will the rate constant be $2k$?
questions.solution_md: $\log 2 = \dfrac{70000}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left(\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$; $\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{T_2} \approx \dfrac{0.301}{3656} \approx 8.234 \times 10^{-5}$; $\dfrac{1}{T_2} \approx 3.3333 \times 10^{-3} - 8.234 \times 10^{-5} \approx 3.2510 \times 10^{-3}$; $T_2 \approx 1 \div 0.0032510 \approx 307.6$, so about $307.6\ \text{K}$.

questions.stem_md: For a reaction with $E_\text{a} = 57.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, calculate the fraction of molecules having energy at least $E_\text{a}$ at $300\ \text{K}$, in units of $10^{-10}$.
Write the Arrhenius equation for the rate constant of the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and explain the significance of A and of the term e^(−Ea/RT).

answer.model_answer_md: k = A e^(−Ea/RT). A is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor, related to the frequency of collisions with proper orientation; it has the same unit as k. The term e^(−Ea/RT) is the fraction of molecules (or collisions) that have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

questions.solution_md: Equation; meaning of A and the exponential.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the activation energy and frequency factor of the decomposition of N₂O₅ can be found from rate constants measured at several temperatures.

answer.model_answer_md: Plot log k against 1/T; from log k = log A − Ea/(2.303RT) the graph is a straight line. Its slope equals −Ea/2.303R, so Ea = −2.303R × slope; the intercept on the log k axis (at 1/T = 0) equals log A, so A = antilog of the intercept.

questions.solution_md: Slope and intercept of log k vs 1/T.

questions.stem_md: The spoiling of milk has an activation energy of about 50 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate how many times more slowly milk spoils in a refrigerator at 278 K than on a kitchen shelf at 303 K.

answer.model_answer_md: $\log\dfrac{k_{303}}{k_{278}} = \dfrac{50000}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{25}{278 \times 303} \approx 2611 \times 2.968 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.775$; ratio $\approx 10^{0.775} \approx 6$. Milk spoils about 6 times more slowly in the refrigerator.

questions.solution_md: About 6 times.

questions.stem_md: The rate constant for the decomposition of a dye in solution is 1.6 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 310 K and 6.4 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 330 K. Calculate the activation energy. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

answer.model_answer_md: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \log 4 = 0.602$; $\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2} = \dfrac{20}{310 \times 330} \approx 1.955 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.602}{1.955 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 58\,960\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, about $59.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: About 59.0 kJ/mol.

questions.stem_md: The decomposition of a pesticide in soil has Ea = 85 kJ mol⁻¹ and k = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ at 300 K. Calculate k at 320 K, and comment on what this suggests for pesticide persistence in hot weather.

answer.model_answer_md: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{85000}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{300 \times 320} \approx 4439 \times 2.083 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.925$; ratio $\approx 8.4$; $k_2 \approx 8.4 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-5} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. The pesticide breaks down about eight times faster at 320 K, so it persists for a much shorter time in hot weather.

questions.solution_md: k ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; faster breakdown.

questions.stem_md: At body temperature (310 K) an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction from 70 kJ mol⁻¹ to 45 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the factor by which the rate increases, assuming A is unchanged. (b) Explain why the enzyme does not change the equilibrium position of the reaction.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\log\dfrac{k_\text{cat}}{k} = \dfrac{25000}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 310} \approx \dfrac{25000}{5936} \approx 4.21$; factor $\approx 10^{4.21} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{4}$.

(b) The enzyme lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction by the same amount, so both rate constants increase by the same factor; their ratio, the equilibrium constant, is unchanged.

questions.solution_md: About 1.6 × 10⁴; equal effect on both directions.

questions.stem_md: Show, using the Arrhenius equation, that a temperature coefficient of 2 between 298 K and 308 K corresponds to an activation energy of about 53 kJ mol⁻¹. Would a reaction with Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹ have a larger or smaller temperature coefficient?

answer.model_answer_md: $\log 2 = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R} \times \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}$, so $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.301 \times 298 \times 308}{10} \approx 52\,900\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 53\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Since $\log(k_2/k_1)$ is proportional to $E_\text{a}$, a reaction with $E_\text{a} = 100\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ would have a larger temperature coefficient (about 3.7).

questions.solution_md: About 53 kJ/mol; larger coefficient.

marking_scheme.step: Larger temperature coefficient for larger Ea

questions.stem_md: The rate constant of the hydrolysis of an alkyl halide is 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and 1.0 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ at 330 K. Calculate (a) the activation energy and (b) the frequency factor A.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 1$; $\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2} = \dfrac{30}{300 \times 330} \approx 3.030 \times 10^{-4}$; $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 1}{3.030 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 63\,190\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, about $63.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

(b) $\log A = \log k_1 + \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303RT_1} = -3 + \dfrac{63190}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300} \approx -3 + 11.0 = 8.0$; $A \approx 1.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Ea ≈ 63.2 kJ/mol; A ≈ 10⁸ s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the Arrhenius equation and its logarithmic form. Explain how a graph can be used to find Ea and A. [2]

(b) The rate constant for the decomposition of hydrogen iodide is 2.15 × 10⁻⁸ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 556 K and 3.95 × 10⁻⁶ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 629 K. Calculate the activation energy. (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $k = Ae^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$; $\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303RT}$. A plot of log k against 1/T is a straight line of slope $-E_\text{a}/2.303R$ (giving Ea) and intercept log A (giving A).

(b) $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \log\dfrac{3.95 \times 10^{-6}}{2.15 \times 10^{-8}} = \log 183.7 \approx 2.264$. $\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2} = \dfrac{73}{556 \times 629} \approx 2.087 \times 10^{-4}$. $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 2.264}{2.087 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 207\,700\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, about $208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Equation and graph; about 208 kJ/mol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the temperature coefficient of a reaction and state its usual value. [1]

(b) The rate constant of a reaction at 300 K is 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ and its activation energy is 75.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate (i) the rate constant at 310 K, (ii) the temperature coefficient and (iii) the time taken for half the reactant to react at 310 K, assuming first-order kinetics. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The ratio of the rate constants at two temperatures differing by 10 K (usually $k_{308}/k_{298}$); usually 2 to 3.

(b) (i) $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{75000}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{10}{300 \times 310} \approx 3917 \times 1.075 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.421$; ratio $\approx 2.64$; $k_2 \approx 2.64 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.055 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. (ii) Temperature coefficient $\approx 2.64$. (iii) $t_{1/2} = 0.693 \div (1.055 \times 10^{-3}) \approx 657\ \text{s}$.

questions.solution_md: Definition; 1.055 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; 2.64; about 657 s.
